ai.title: AI-Powered Predictions — How Accurate Are We?
ai.subtitle: park.fan uses its own AI model trained on millions of real queue records to forecast crowd levels and wait times at theme parks worldwide. The model factors in weather forecasts, school holiday calendars, and known events — and retrains automatically as fresh data arrives.
ai.avgErrorDesc: MAE — how many minutes off our predictions are on average
ai.rmseDesc: RMSE — how bad the worst misses are, outliers weighted more
ai.mapeDesc: MAPE — percentage error relative to actual wait time

ai.modelAgeHours: Model trained {time} hours ago · automatically retrained on new data
ai.howText: Every wait time forecast is built from three layers of data: historical queue records collected from parks over years, external signals like weather forecasts and school holiday calendars, and contextual factors such as special events and seasonal patterns. The model generates both hourly wait time forecasts for individual rides and daily crowd level ratings for full park visits — available up to 365 days ahead.
ai.fancastLink: How Fancast, our forecasting model, works
ai.improvingText: park.fan is a living platform, still in active development. Every day the system automatically compares its earlier predictions against the wait times actually recorded at the parks, feeding those comparisons back into the next training cycle. The accuracy metrics above reflect this real-world performance — not synthetic benchmarks. New parks and attractions are added regularly, and the model becomes more accurate as it accumulates more verified data for each destination.

about.title: What Is park.fan?
about.p1: park.fan was born from a frustration every theme park fan knows: standing in a 90-minute queue and wondering whether smarter planning could have avoided it. What started as a side project—"let me just track some wait times"—grew into a full platform now covering 212 parks, 7,101 attractions, and millions of queue data records processed every day. The goal has always been the same: take the guesswork out of planning a theme park visit.
about.p2: The AI behind park.fan analyzes historical crowd data, weather forecasts, school holiday calendars, and special events to predict crowd levels and wait times days or even weeks ahead. Instead of guessing, you can check whether next Saturday at Europa-Park Resort or Phantasialand is going to be a green day—short queues, relaxed atmosphere—or a red day where every popular ride has a 60-minute wait. The model is continuously trained on new data, so its predictions get sharper over time.
about.p3: park.fan currently tracks 212 theme parks and 7,101 individual attractions worldwide—from Walt Disney World, Disneyland Resort, Universal Orlando, and Universal Studios Japan to European parks like Europa-Park, Phantasialand, Efteling, Heide Park, and Toverland, plus parks across Asia, Australia, and South America. New parks are added regularly as the platform continues to grow.
about.p4: Search for your destination park using the search bar, or browse by continent, country, and city. On the park page you will find live wait times for every ride, restaurant, and show—updated every minute—alongside AI crowd predictions and a day-by-day crowd calendar. Green days signal short queues and smaller crowds; orange or red days mean higher attendance and longer waits.
about.p5: park.fan is a living project, constantly evolving with new features and parks. Save your favourite parks for quick access, use in-park navigation to plan the most efficient route through the park, and always check the crowd calendar before booking to make sure your visit lands on the best possible day.

steps.title: Three steps to a well-planned park day
steps.lead: Pick a park, check the day, plan the route. park.fan brings measurements from more than 200 parks to each of the three.

one.title: Pick a park
one.text: Type the park or the ride, or take the suggestion near you. Every park has its own page with live wait times, opening hours and a calendar.
one.tip: The search finds more than parks. If you know you want to ride Taron but not which park it stands in, just type the ride’s name. Shows and restaurants are in there too.
one.label: Search for a park or ride

two.title: Check the day
two.text: The crowd calendar rates every day up to 365 days ahead: green means short queues, red means packed walkways and long detours.
two.tip: Two days next to each other are often two different parks. If the date is yours to choose, look at the week before and after before you book.
two.caption: A month in the calendar: one tile per day, the colour is the crowd level expected.

three.title: Plan the route
three.text: Every ride comes with its best window, so you are not queueing for the headliner at the midday peak.
three.tip: “Get there early” does not hold for every ride. Some run just as full all day, others only pick up after lunch. Each ride’s own page carries its own day curve.
three.caption: A coaster’s typical day, from opening to evening.
three.best: The quietest windows sit early and in the last hour.

nearby.title: Theme parks near you
nearby.lead: Share your location and park.fan shows the parks around you: whether they are open today, how busy it is right now and how long the average queue is.

live.title: Wait times for every ride, refreshed every five minutes
live.lead: For every attraction and every queue type, plus opening hours and breakdowns.
live.body: We show not just the number but what it means: 95 minutes is a lot on a Tuesday in September and perfectly normal on a Saturday in October. That is why every ride page says what is typical for that weekday and what a busy day looks like.
live.ridesTitle: Every ride has its own page
live.ridesText: Thousands of ride pages, each with what holds for that one ride: queue types, the day’s course from measurement and forecast, typical times by weekday, height limit and a rope-drop tip.
live.ropeDropText: Head here at opening: on the popular rides the first hour is regularly the shortest window of the day.
live.howtoLink: How to read a wait time: the guide

shows.title: A park day is not only roller coasters
shows.lead: park.fan lists shows and restaurants too: the day’s show times, plus the cuisine, the opening hours and whether a table has to be booked.
shows.showsHint: Every performance of the day with its time, the next one first, and whether the show is currently in season.
shows.restaurantsHint: Cuisine, opening hours and whether booking is required, so the hunt for a table does not start in the middle of the best riding hours.
shows.body: A three o’clock performance pulls a few thousand people out of the queues and puts them back afterwards. Knowing the show times means you can spend the half hour before it at a ride instead of in the theatre.

calendar.title: A green day or a red one?
calendar.lead: Before you book the hotel: the calendar rates every single day, up to 365 days ahead. Where a day’s colour comes from is set out below.
calendar.pipelineTitle: From the measurement to the colour of a day
calendar.pipelineLead: Four steps, redone every night. Whatever ends up in the calendar as a green or a red day took this path.

p1.title: Measure
p1.text: Every five minutes park.fan polls the parks’ queue systems: standby, single rider, Lightning Lane, virtual queues, plus the operating status of every ride.
p1.label: Measurement interval

p2.title: Collect
p2.text: Every reading is archived with its timestamp, ride and park. Years of them give each ride a profile of its own: the course of a day, the rhythm of a week, the season.
p2.label: Records

p3.title: Enrich
p3.text: Signals from outside join in: the weather forecast, school and public holidays from the countries the parks stand in, bridge days, and special events like Halloween or the start of the season.
p3.label: Holidays, weather

p4.title: Forecast
p4.text: Fancast turns all of that into an expected wait per ride and per hour, then condenses it into the day’s crowd level, which is the colour you see in the calendar.
p4.label: Days ahead

calendar.feedback: The next day every forecast is laid against the wait time actually measured. The difference goes into the next round of training, and that is why the calendar colour for one and the same day changes as the day gets closer.
calendar.body: Green days mean short queues and room to move. Orange and red mean every popular ride costs you three quarters of an hour. To get there the calendar weighs holiday calendars, weather forecasts, weekdays and special events against the park’s real wait-time history.
calendar.bestTimeLink: Best time to visit: the quietest weekdays and months

ai.title: A forecast of our own, with the error printed next to it
ai.lead: Predicting wait times is the hard part, and most sites step around it. park.fan takes it on with Fancast, a model of its own, retrained every night, up to 365 days ahead.
ai.compareLead: Three approaches are common, and all three share one blind spot: nobody tells you how far off the forecast was.

c1.title: No forecast at all
c1.text: Germany’s largest wait-time site deliberately does without predictions: too many factors, and a wrong forecast could hurt parks and visitors alike. All it shows is how busy it was.
c1.limit: A look back does not answer “which day do I book?”

c2.title: The average of similar days
c2.text: A statistical model looks for comparable days in the past — same weekday, same holiday situation — and averages them. Usually 90 days ahead and often for a single park only.
c2.limit: Without three comparable days the day stays empty.

c3.title: Statistics plus a bit of AI
c3.text: Ensembles mix statistical analysis with an AI share and factor in holidays and weather, labelled beta, for one park, in steps from “excellent” to “very long”.
c3.limit: With no error figure, what the level is worth stays open.

ai.answerTitle: Fancast forecasts by the hour, per ride – and publishes its error.
ai.answerText: Not one crowd level per day, but the expected wait for each hour. Every forecast is later checked against the real measurement, and the accuracy figures below come out of that.

bestTime.title: Many rides have two quiet windows, in the morning and towards the evening
bestTime.lead: Rope drop does not pay off on every ride. The curve comes from that attraction’s own measured days.
bestTime.chartSubtitle: Median of {days} measured days, sampled every 5 minutes
bestTime.heatText: On hot days the crowd shifts: water rides pick up, indoor dark rides fill, coasters empty out. The calendar takes that into account.
bestTime.historyText: Every ride has a curve of its own, a rhythm of its own across the week and a season of its own. Every reading taken today goes into tomorrow’s model.
bestTime.hubLink: Best time to visit for 200+ parks
bestTime.windowOpening: A good start to the day
bestTime.windowClosing: Towards the end of the day

inPark.title: On the day itself, what counts is 200 metres away
inPark.lead: Before the visit you plan with the calendar and the forecast. In the park you need two things: the rides you saved and the wait times on the park map.
inPark.favText: One tap on the star, on every park, every ride, every show and every restaurant. Your favourites then sit at the top of the homepage with their live wait time and opening status. No account, saved in the browser.
inPark.mapText: Rides, shows and restaurants sit on the park map as coloured markers; a tap shows status, wait time and how busy it is. When park.fan can tell you are in the park, your position joins them and the nearest rides move to the top.

dictionary.title: Zero-G roll, Immelmann, top hat – ride them in the player
dictionary.lead: The park.fan dictionary explains the jargon, and track elements come with a 3-D player: pick a figure, play it, scrub to any point of the ride.

why.title: Six reasons this one works differently

r1.title: Our own model, trained daily
r1.text: No third-party provider, no off-the-shelf black box. The model keeps learning every night from the previous day’s data.

r2.title: The accuracy is published
r2.text: The mean error and the R² value sit on this page and are recalculated after every round of training, good or bad.

r3.title: Every five minutes, not once a day
r3.text: Wait times are merged from three public sources every five minutes. If a ride goes down it says so here before you are standing in front of it.

r4.title: Free, no subscription, no paywall
r4.text: Everything park.fan knows about a park, you get to see as well, without an account and without a paywall.

r5.title: 200+ parks, 23 countries, 6 languages
r5.text: From Phantasialand to Tokyo DisneySea. If there are queues there, we track them.

r6.title: Data that explains something
r6.text: A dictionary, park guides and data pieces on the blog. Why a park is empty in November and packed in October is written up as an article.

founder.title: One developer, one data model of his own, no investor
founder.name: Patrick Arns
founder.p1: park.fan is not a startup with investors and roadmap meetings. It is the project of someone who has been going to theme parks since he was in a pram and building software for over 25 years. The frustration was a concrete one: queueing 90 minutes for a ride and suspecting that a bit of planning would have avoided it.
founder.p2: So first came a tracker, then a database, then a machine-learning system of his own, built end to end from the data import to the forecast and retrained every night.
founder.authorLink: More about Patrick on the blog

attraction.waitTimeA: Wait times for {attraction} vary by day and season. Check live wait times on park.fan.
attraction.waitTimeStatsA: Today the wait for {attraction} averages {avg} minutes, ranging from {min} to {max} minutes. The current live wait time is shown above on this page.

faq.whatIsA: park.fan is your central platform for live wait times and current information from over 200 theme parks in Europe, Asia, and North America. We show you in real-time how long the wait times are at your favorite attractions, which shows are currently running, and when the parks are open.
faq.whichParksQ: Which theme parks are supported by park.fan?
faq.whichParksA: park.fan supports over 200 theme parks worldwide, including Phantasialand, Europa-Park, Disneyland Paris, Efteling, Walibi Belgium, Toverland, Bobbejaanland, and many more. You can find the complete list of all parks with live wait times on our parks overview page. We are continuously expanding our offering with additional theme parks.
faq.liveDataQ: Are the wait times on park.fan live and in real-time?
faq.liveDataA: Yes. Every park is polled every five minutes from three public sources at once – ThemeParks.wiki, Wartezeiten.app and Queue-Times.com. Where two sources disagree, the majority decides, then the median, then the mean. The result is rounded to five minutes, because that is how the parks post them.
faq.freeA: Yes, park.fan is completely free to use. You can view all live wait times, opening hours, shows, and restaurants without registration or payment. Our goal is to provide the best possible service to every theme park visitor.
faq.favoritesQ: Can I save my favorite parks and attractions on park.fan?
faq.favoritesA: Yes! With park.fan’s favorites feature, you can mark your favorite parks and favorite attractions. These will then be displayed on your personalized homepage, so you can immediately see the current wait times for your favorites.
faq.featuresQ: What information does park.fan offer besides live wait times?
faq.featuresA: In addition to live wait times for attractions, park.fan also provides park opening hours, show times, restaurant information, weather forecasts, historical wait time statistics, and crowd forecasts. This way, you can optimally plan your theme park visit and find the best times for your favorite attractions.
faq.mobileA: Absolutely! park.fan is fully responsive and works perfectly on smartphones and tablets. You can check live wait times directly in the theme park to spontaneously decide which attraction to visit next. The mobile version offers all features of the desktop version.
